title: Working with Development Teams
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Working with Development Teams.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Working with Development Teams and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Working with Development Teams, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 26: Professional Practice and Career Development. It builds practical understanding of Working with Development Teams with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Working with Development Teams helps communicate security outcomes in a way development and operations teams can act on. Identify assets, actors, entry points, data flows, and trust boundaries; prioritize realistic threats and record mitigations as testable requirements.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Working with Development Teams can be understood through this sequence: Capture operational signal → Protect sensitive context → Assign accountable owner → Review and improve. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 190.1 Security requirements in planning; 190.2 Developer-friendly remediation advice; 190.3 Collaborative code reviews; 190.4 Integrating feedback into secure design; 190.5 Resolving security findings before release. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Identify assets, actors, entry points, data flows, and trust boundaries; prioritize realistic threats and record mitigations as testable requirements.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.code:
Topic: Working with Development Teams
Review artifact: define scope, assumptions, control owner, expected secure behavior, failure behavior, and a reproducible verification step.
content_blocks.expected_output: A written review artifact names the control and the evidence needed to verify it.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a local/owned application or explicitly authorized test target. Record only sanitized synthetic evidence; use human review for behavior that a static snippet cannot prove.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Identify assets, actors, entry points, data flows, and trust boundaries; prioritize realistic threats and record mitigations as testable requirements. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Working with Development Teams”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Working with Development Teams in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Working with Development Teams is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Identify assets, actors, entry points, data flows, and trust boundaries; prioritize realistic threats and record mitigations as testable requirements.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
